# Progress this week (5/10-5/15) ---
New Extraction Prompts **Three levels of quality filtering**: ---
Low Quality ``` Extract the content from this HTML page as clean text. Follow all rules below. 1. Extract the full page content in reading order. Keep all explanatory text, discussion, and comments that add substantive information. Begin your output directly with the page content. 2. Remove boilerplate: navigation bars, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs, cookie banners, and user interface elements. Do not output framework markers or metadata tags. 3. Preserve all technical content exactly as written: code, math notation, formulas, tables, and data. Preserve the original line breaks and structure of code blocks. 4. Decode all HTML entities to their plain characters (e.g. & to &, < to <, > to >, ’ to ', – to –). Remove any raw HTML tags. 5. Every sentence in your output must come from the source page. Do not add, invent, or embellish content. 6. For pages with multiple authors or speakers (forums, reviews, comments), preserve who said what. Include usernames or speaker labels so contributions remain distinguishable. 7. If the text contains content spinner templates like {word1|word2|word3}, pick the first option and output clean text. If the majority of the page is spinner templates, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] instead. 8. Output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] if ANY of these apply:    - Login, signup, paywall, registration wall, or "you must sign up to view" page    - Error page, empty page, or cookie/captcha wall    - Terms of use, privacy policy, or legal boilerplate page    - User profile page with no substantive content    - Page whose content has been removed, moved, or is no longer available    - Image gallery, photo album listing, or media archive without articles    - The text is incoherent gibberish or garbled encoding throughout    - The page has under ~50 words of substantive content after removing boilerplate    However, for index pages or directory listings, only filter if they contain nothing but links and titles. If an index page includes real text like discussion snippets or descriptions, extract it. ```
---
Medium Quality ``` Extract the content from this HTML page as clean text. Apply all rules below. 1. **Quality bar.** The page must be real written content — coherent prose that conveys information, ideas, narrative, or experience. Acceptable: articles, explanations, analyses, reviews with substantive commentary, tutorials, manuals, reference entries, documentation, and substantive forum or comment discussions. If the page does not pass, output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT].    **Walk through each bullet below in order**, checking whether the page matches it. If any bullet applies, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and do not extract.    - **Navigation or aggregation** — exists to point elsewhere (forum indexes, category pages, tag clouds, search results, sitemaps, archive-by-date pages, contributor lists, topic-aggregation pages of one-line summaries). A tag archive showing one truncated post excerpt still fails — the page must contain at least one full post.    - **Site machinery** — login, signup, paywall, cookie banner, captcha, error page, "page not found", redirect notice, terms of service, privacy policy, subscription/notification form ("send to a friend", email signup), or instructions for using the site itself. Pages whose main content is hidden behind a login wall fail even when the page shows a "you must be logged in" prompt.    - **Fragments** — Tumblr-style image-reblog streams, social timelines, photo-blog feeds, lists of one-liner microposts, image gallery captions, personal "about me" pages, and repost stubs that consist of a brief excerpt plus a "Read on:", "Go to Source", "View original", or affiliate link to elsewhere. Pages of fragments and metadata rather than coherent passages.    - **Wrapper around non-textual media** — a video, audio, slideshow, photo, or interactive widget where the page exists to host the media rather than be read. Includes image-only social posts (Blingee/Pinterest-style), single-photo pages with a one-line caption, video-player pages with only a title/byline around the video, and blog posts whose body is a short reaction (a sentence or two) around an embedded video, image, or share.    - **Commerce or product page** — pages with prices, availability, "Add to Cart", or shipping/stock indicators. Vendor-written descriptions, specs, ingredients, and care instructions are commerce metadata, not content — they do not save the page. Keep only if the page contains an extended editorial passage about the product (a third-party review, comparison, or analysis), not vendor sales copy. Also includes **employer or company profile pages** ("Quick Look", "Company Overview") that are mostly company name, industry, size, and a bullet list of services or job categories.    - **Raw data dump** — structured data without surrounding narrative. This includes both rows of data (rosters, statistics tables, file indexes, contact directories, database exports) **and single-record entries** (museum specimen cards, IP whois / BGP route lookups, dictionary entries that are only a definition line, badge / user-profile / member pages). An article that uses tables to support its prose is fine.    - **Too short** — count the substantive sentences on the page after removing boilerplate, navigation, ads, comments, links, dates, and reposted excerpts. **If the remaining substantive prose is fewer than 5 complete sentences, the page fails.** Apply this strictly: a 1-paragraph news brief, a 2-sentence "X just opened in Y" announcement, a single-event calendar entry, "this section has moved" notice, "no results found" / "no products matching" / "click here to proceed" placeholder — all fail, regardless of how grammatical or informative-looking the few sentences are.    - **Incoherent** — gibberish, garbled encoding, machine-translated nonsense, or spinner templates throughout. First determine if the page clears the quality bar. If it does, follow the following rules to extract the content. 2. **Extract the full page content in reading order**. Keep explanatory text, discussion, and comments that add substantive information. Begin your output directly with the page content. 3. **Remove boilerplate**: navigation, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs, cookie banners, and UI elements. Do not output framework markers or metadata tags. 4. **Preserve all technical content** exactly as written: code, math, formulas, tables, and data. Preserve original line breaks and the structure of code blocks. 5. Decode HTML entities to plain characters (e.g. & → &, ’ → '). Remove raw HTML tags. 6. **Do not add, invent, or embellish content.** Every sentence must come from the source page. 7. For pages with multiple authors or speakers (forums, reviews, comments), preserve who said what — include usernames or speaker labels. 8. If the page contains content spinner templates like {word1|word2|word3}, pick the first option. If most of the page is spinners, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]. ```
---
High Quality ``` Extract the content from this HTML page as clean text. Apply all rules below. 1. **EXTREME quality bar — keep almost nothing.** This filter is designed to retain only the very best educational and informative content; only about 1 in 10 pages should pass. The **default is to output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]**.    **HARD GATES — check first, in order. If any gate fails, immediately output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and stop.**    - **Gate A — Language.** Is the body of the page written primarily in English? If the main prose is in any other language (French, Spanish, German, Chinese, Russian, etc.), output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]. Quoted phrases, names, citations, or short snippets in another language are fine; a page whose main prose is non-English is not — even if the topic looks substantive.    - **Gate B — Prose depth.** Are there roughly 300 or more words of real *prose* — flowing sentences and paragraphs that explain, argue, or teach? Table cells, formula tokens, code-only listings, navigation labels, whois fields, stat lines, and metadata do NOT count toward the word budget. A page that hits 300 "words" only by counting structured-data fields fails this gate.    A page that clears both gates is kept ONLY if all four of these are also true:    - **Teaches the reader.** The page explains a concept, mechanism, method, or topic; develops an argument with evidence and examples; reports original analysis; or delivers substantive technical or instructional material. It must convey real knowledge of the world, not just headlines, facts, or summaries.    - **Carefully written.** Clear, structured, professional or academic-quality prose. Not casual, not fragmentary, not marketing copy, not auto-generated, not template-filled.    - **Self-contained value.** A reader who lands here learns meaningfully from this page alone — not from clicking through to something else.    - **Not matched by any FAILS bullet below.**    **Walk through each FAILS bullet below in order**, checking whether the page matches it. If any matches, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and do not extract.    Categories that typically qualify (still subject to all criteria above):    - Long-form journalism with original reporting and analysis — including editorial tech journalism or product reporting that includes quotes, context, history, or analysis (even when the subject is a company's product launch)    - Educational or explanatory articles (science, math, history, engineering, medicine, philosophy, economics, etc.)    - Tutorials, how-tos, and documentation with real teaching — instructions plus the reasoning behind them    - Encyclopedia and reference entries written with substantive prose    - **Substantive technical forum, mailing-list, or Q&A threads** — e.g., a Stack Overflow question with a thorough accepted answer, a numpy/scipy mailing-list discussion working through a real problem, a developer forum thread that reaches a meaningful technical conclusion. The "casual forum threads" FAILS bullet does NOT apply when the discussion is technical and develops the topic.    - Research papers, white papers, technical writeups    - Essays and analyses that develop an argument with evidence — including substantive opinion or commentary on a personal blog or social platform like Tumblr/Medium/Substack    - Code accompanied by genuine teaching, not just a snippet    - Technical blogs sharing real domain expertise    - Institutional or organizational descriptions with substantive prose (academic program pages with curriculum and outcomes, organizational reports, conference or event summaries with real narrative)    - Religious or scriptural texts presenting substantive narrative or doctrine (e.g., a Bible chapter, Quran sura, philosophical canon — numbered-verse format is fine)    Categories that FAIL — filter even if the writing is fine:    - **News briefs, sports recaps, and transaction roundups** — "X happened, said Y" reporting without analysis, depth, or context. Includes local sports recaps ("West Side beat Cumberland 14-4"), team transaction logs ("Signed pitcher X to a minor-league contract"), and short news items even when several are stitched together on one page.    - **Personal lifestyle or diary blogging** — daily-life updates, travelogues, opinion pieces without intellectual substance. (A personal blog with substantive analysis or argument is fine — judge by content, not platform.)    - **Light reviews — including aggregator pages of light reviews** — "I tried it, it's good" without genuine analysis or comparison. A page that strings together several short product blurbs is still light reviews, not substantive content.    - **Reference stubs and structured-data dumps** — one-paragraph wiki entries, definitions, factoid lists, player stat cards, whois/BGP/DNS records, raw lookup results, single-formula pages. If the page is mostly a table, a record, or one isolated fact, it fails — fastText-style classifiers may rate this content highly because it "looks structured," but it is not teaching prose.    - **Casual forum threads** — chit-chat, brief Q&A without resolution, social exchanges that don't reach a meaningful conclusion. Technical mailing-list or Q&A threads that DO develop the topic are covered by the qualifying bullet above and are NOT this.    - **Vendor sales copy or purely promotional material** — product descriptions, ad copy, "buy now" pages. (Institutional descriptions of academic programs, mission statements with real content, organizational reports, or editorial journalism about a product launch are NOT this; judge by whether the page sells a product or describes/teaches.)    - **Mostly un-decoded HTML / escape soup** — pages where the visible text is dominated by raw HTML entities (` `, `<`, `&`, `&#NNN;`), escape sequences, or malformed markup that survived the page render. Even if the underlying content might be code or text, a page presented this way is junk for training.    - **"No results" / search-empty pages** — "your search returned no results", "no items match", "0 records found" — even when they list related links or alternative searches alongside.    - **Anything that fails a normal quality filter** — commerce pages, navigation or aggregation surfaces, login walls or other site machinery, fragments and microposts, wrappers around non-textual media, raw data dumps, empty placeholders, incoherent text    **When in doubt, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT].** Reject borderline pages aggressively; only clear winners pass. First determine if the page clears the EXTREME quality bar. If it does, follow the following rules to extract the content. 2. **Extract the full page content in reading order**. Keep explanatory text, discussion, and comments that add substantive information. Begin your output directly with the page content. 3. **Remove boilerplate**: navigation, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs, cookie banners, and UI elements. Do not output framework markers or metadata tags. 4. **Preserve all technical content** exactly as written: code, math, formulas, tables, and data. Preserve original line breaks and the structure of code blocks. 5. Decode HTML entities to plain characters (e.g. & → &, ’ → '). Remove raw HTML tags. 6. **Do not add, invent, or embellish content.** Every sentence must come from the source page. 7. For pages with multiple authors or speakers (forums, reviews, comments), preserve who said what — include usernames or speaker labels. 8. If the page contains content spinner templates like {word1|word2|word3}, pick the first option. If most of the page is spinners, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]. ```
--- Using these prompts I have gotten the following distributions of tokens: Looks even better than DCLM **and** with more tokens: Unfortunately higher budget jobs have been queued for a little while. ---
How did I settle on these prompts? Only works if hosted: [http://localhost:8090/?show_token=dclm%3Adclm_full&show_token=dclm%3Av15_then_dclm_full&show_token=curator%3Acurator_general_v15&show_token=curator%3Acurator_quality_v8&show_token=curator%3Acurator_extreme_v5&url=&sort=record_index&reverse=0&state.dclm=&state.dclm_full=&state.v15_then_dclm_full=&state.curator_general_v15=&state.curator_quality_v8=&state.curator_extreme_v5=](http://localhost:8090/?show_token=dclm%3Adclm_full&show_token=dclm%3Av15_then_dclm_full&show_token=curator%3Acurator_general_v15&show_token=curator%3Acurator_quality_v8&show_token=curator%3Acurator_extreme_v5&url=&sort=record_index&reverse=0&state.dclm=&state.dclm_full=&state.v15_then_dclm_full=&state.curator_general_v15=&state.curator_quality_v8=&state.curator_extreme_v5=) Observing how random sample of 1k documents was extracted by each.
--- Not too long before I finish scaling up the high quality prompt: This has also been slightly problematic for cluster contention so we are redesigning the distributed inference stack: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1UEnIabqLPrjfYfSDGqQVad252nLETi8L9MeBvh81YoY/edit?tab=t.xe6eofm9ervd#heading=h.46dj0uyi8n53 ---
---
Deduplication Deduplication ended up being pretty important! Now all my experiments with resiliparse and llm_extracted are using deduplication: ``` Exact dedup runs inside marin.datakit.normalize.normalize_step with DedupMode.EXACT — it drops byte-identical documents by xxh3_128 hash of the text field (one hex id per record). Fuzzy dedup then runs MinHash-LSH connected-components on top with 286 permutations / 26 bands / 5-char ngrams / seed 42 / ~0.75 Jaccard threshold, keeping one canonical doc per cluster (see experiments/baseline_collection/dedup_extracted.py:380-419). ``` Dedupe was even important for the **high_quality** filter because of sites like this: And there are sometimes articles are posted multiple times: [file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/marin/scratch/clusters_high_quality_100.html](file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/marin/scratch/clusters_high_quality_100.html)
---
Scaling Plan Once I have this plot for **low_quality**, **med_quality** (maybe), and **high_quality**. [http://localhost:8091/plots/eval_lima_loss/grid_compressed_x_tokens_all_epochs.html](http://localhost:8091/plots/eval_lima_loss/grid_compressed_x_tokens_all_epochs.html) Then I will use the [Meunninghoff et al.](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.16264) scaling laws to figure out how we should expect each data source to scale with epoching. Where N' and D' are the discounted tokens and parameters from epoching or training excess parameters. Then I get a relationship where I can predict loss from a given parameter and compute budget and can make a plot like this: **NOTE I don't think I've fit this quite right yet, so don't trust this exact plot but this is meant to serve as an example:** My plan would be to show the tradeoff between high_quality, med_quality, and low_quality perhaps both at the literal compute budget we train at AND if you were to scale up to training trillion parameter models. The argument would be this is something you could do at small scales to predict what dataset you should use when you scale up.
---
Next Steps - Finish Extracting **High_Quality** spec docs (1-2 days) - Train Scaling Ladder for High_Quality spec (3 days) - Run CORE evals on the lowest loss config with every dataset (ensuring that val loss was a predictive measure) (hours) - (Optional) Run Extraction on **Med_quality** spec (6-7 days) - Plot the tradeoff of parameters and compute versus what dataset you should use. (bottlenecked by me figuring this out)
---
Beyond the Paper I think one particularly promising idea would be if we truly are getting higher quality data than DCLM at 4x the tokens, this would be worth making a case for trying to scale up to actually run this closer to internet scale. One potential path: - If we end up locking in a specific spec we could distill an even smaller model on just that spec. We actually have a ton of data now to do this and might even be possible to train a model from scratch! - We would need to secure more compute for this... Right now extracting 3k WARCs takes 6 days (optimistically). Extracting 8 million WARCs would thus take (8M / 3k = 2666 * 6 days = 16,000 days / 365 = ~43.84 years) about 44 years. I think by distilling a smaller model we can dramatically reduce that but probably would be a combination of that plus more compute. - The other question is if this is worth the squeeze versus just generating synthetic data or something else.
---

# Progress this week (6/1-6/5) Paper draft is looking good :) Main points for discussion today: - Is my approach for fixing the sampling issue satisfactory? - Planning the scale up timeline and strategy. - Plan for scientific paper versus bigger pretraining data project. ---
Paper is done! Overleaf: [https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4](https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4) We evaluate models on RealToxicityPrompts \cite{gehman-etal-2020-realtoxicityprompts} judged by Detoxity \cite{Detoxify} and find 2.9B models trained on our **High-Quality extraction only produce toxic completions on 3.3\% of prompts compared to 5.1\% with DCLM**. One thing that is missing is Decontamination. I still need to run Decontamination.
---
The sampling issue There are three ways to resolve the sampling issue. I think one makes more sense for the paper and the other we will get for free as we start to scale up. **Option A: ** Extract the 10,364 WARC files that make up the DCLM 400m-1x pool with our high quality Spec. This is a RANDOM sample of WARC files but it is limited to 2013-2022 (Nemotron-CC goes until 2024). For our scaling experiments we leave the biased sample and make that clear (don't re-extract "low-quality" and "medium-quality" spec). Pros: Directly comparable to DCLM. In fact we will get to upload to the DCLM leaderboard. Any sampling bias can be attributed to DCLM's choices. Also gives us more useful extracted data than rerunning all specs at all scales. Cons: Still somewhat biased against Nemotron-CC. Still takes 2 weeks to run. The biased sample was provably harmful for nemotron: I think ultimately we can do a completely unbiased sample versus nemotron once I start to scale up to the whole common crawl with my more efficient method (more on this later), but perhaps this is good for the "scientific" writeup? **Option B: ** Re-extract a completely random sample with all extractors for fair comparison to Nemotron-CC. This means we cannot compare to DCLM (cutoff 2022). About the same 2 week timeline (maybe 2.5 weeks) **Option C: ** Just extract random 3k sample from the DCLM range with all methods. Same timeline, but not really new useful data and we still know we are biased against nemotron by missing 2022-2024.
---
Distilling the full "Spec-Driven Extraction Pipeline" Two Main things I need to achieve: 1. Distill the CONTENT FILTERING decision into a single fastText classifier. 2. Distill a Single-Spec into a much smaller LLM given that we no longer care about swapping the spec. 3. Reduce the size of the input prompts to the LLM extractor stage ### Single Filter FastText Classifier Pretty good success so far! Training a fastText classifier on about 13M documents that our Spec-Driven curator made decisions on yields a model that can retain 95% of useful content while dropping 79% of junk content! This will hopefully lead to an 80% cost reduction with only a slight quality reduction. ### Distill a Single Spec Model Less progress here so far. Kicked off some Qwen3-0.6B runs based on data from 2930 WARC extractions with the High Quality spec. ALSO trying to remove reasoning now that we are doing single spec and a lot of the reasoning had to do with whether or not we extract the content. Reasoning was accounting for **3x as many tokens as extraction** (this includes on filtered rows though which explains part of the problem. Benchmarking GPT-OSS versus our 8B extractor in the single spec setting. This is where I will compare Qwen3-0.6b when SFT is done. ### Reduce the size of the inputs to the Model I realized that I was running the extractor on the FULL HTML which is great for the paper (super clean story) but bad for throughput. Now I am stripping to just the body tag and removing script tags which we showed worked earlier but I accidentally didn't do for our production runs. This leads to a median 21% reduction in the size of the input that gets to the model. ### Speedup Assuming: - 80% time reduction from FastText - 20% time reduction from input size reduction - 40% time reduction from dropping reasoning and smaller model (pretty much a guess) New pipeline should take 9.6% of the time to process, but I still need to benchmark. This isn't good enough.... that brings us from 42 years down to 4.2 Years. I need to be 563 times faster to bring things from 42 years down to 1 month.
---

# Progress this week (6/15-6/19) --- Key Question: **How should I fairly run DCLM COREv2 Evals on these models when there is token count/quality mismatch?**
Random WARC Extraction Took the full DCLM 400M-1x Data Pool. We now have a competition ready compatible submission for DCLM **Old results**: **New results**:
---
Decontamination [file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/marin/scratch/decon_inspect_n15.html](file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/marin/scratch/decon_inspect_n15.html) A document was removed if it contained even a single 15-word-gram that also appears in a DCLM CORE v2 eval item — provided that 15-gram is distinctive (appears in ≤10 eval-source docs).
--- Key Question: **What signs of life should I prioritize on the fast data curation pipeline to be sure this is working well at scale?**
Pipeline Improvements ---
Rule Based Heuristics Expressed each DCLM and custom HTML rule as a tunable threshold on a single feature, then greedily assembled them under a hard recall ≥ 0.99 constraint: at each step we add the threshold that discards the most no_useful documents per unit of useful lost, stopping once the ~1% recall budget is spent.
---
FastText + ModernBERT Usefulness Classifier Cascade **fastText (stage 1)**: Trained as a binary "useful vs [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]" classifier on ~2.46M raw body_strip HTML docs (189k useful + 2.27M non-useful, the 12:1 deployment ratio) from 80 WARCs across 24 CC snapshots, using the hand-set DCLM bigram recipe (epoch 5, lr 0.1, dim 100, wordNgrams 2, softmax). Pruning with --min count 500 shrank it to a sub-GB model (0.96 GB) at full quality (F1 0.594). **ModernBERT (stage 2)**: Fine-tuned answerdotai/ModernBERT-base (8192 ctx) on the same target but over 1M docs sampled only from the fastText survivor pool, on TPU v6e-4 with PyTorch + torch_xla in bf16 (effective batch 256, lr 5e-5, 1 epoch). Training on the survivor residual specialized it for exactly the deployment distribution, lifting standalone F1 to 0.705 and giving the best high-recall operating point in the cascade.
---
jusText Custom Extractor Fork AutoResearched it! Each cycle, we sampled the worst-scoring documents on the dev set, found a recurring fixable artifact (forum/comment/FAQ structure, code/URL/encoding mangling, list/dash formatting), fixed it in justext/core.py, and re-measured against the baseline across all five datasets — shipping only changes with no real regression and logging each in research_log/. On top of ~70 such structural fixes we layered a learned paragraph classifier (RandomForest stacked with a fastText keep-probability model), and validated the whole thing once on the held-out test split at the end to confirm we generalized rather than overfit. [https://github.com/XenonMolecule/jusText](https://github.com/XenonMolecule/jusText) [file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/jusText/benchmark/runs/current-cmarker/general/dev.report.html](file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/jusText/benchmark/runs/current-cmarker/general/dev.report.html) [dev.report.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29150650/dev.report.html)
---
FastText Router The jusText-extractability router is a fastText classifier that predicts, from a raw doc, whether a cheap jusText extraction will land within 0.85 normalized Levenshtein similarity of the gold LLM extraction (i.e. ≥85% character-identical) — labeling such docs "extractable" (→ jusText) and everything else, including all [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] abstentions, as "needs LLM" (→ 1.7B/gpt-oss-120b). Because only ~5.5% of docs naturally clear that strict bar, at its F1-optimal threshold the router sends just ~8% of survivors (3,381 of 41,245 ≈ 1.9% of all raw docs) to jusText and leaves the remaining ~92% (37,864 docs) on the expensive model path, offloading less than a tenth of the extraction workload.

The main thing is I didn't realize **we were still relying on scale to win**. We were **not Pareto dominant at DCLM evals even at the 3k scale** and this was hidden by evaluating only on the points that had minimum val loss on uncheatable eval. Compute matched we were losing.
---
Where are the gaps/successes in our data? ### uncheatable eval: **AO3 (Fanfiction)** **BBC News** **Github Python** **Wikipedia (English)** **Github C++** **arXiv CS** **arXiv Physics** ### Olmo: **QA_bpb** **Code_bpb** **Math_bpb** ### Full Dashboard: Locally: file:///Users/michaelryan/Documents/School/Stanford/Research/marin/scratch/plots/subcomponents_10k/subcomponents_dashboard.html Unfortunately too big to host this html on GitHub :( ### Takeaways: We are better at code, and pretty on par with others at math/wikipedia language modeling. At scale we are pretty good at arxiv, but not Pareto dominant. Our real gaps are fiction, qa benchmarks, and to some extent news articles. This informs some of the areas we need to improve on.
---
New Devset (and ways of measuring spec quality) **Labelled a Devset of 935 docs so far (999 to go, but seeing if claude can help)** Labelled it for keep, weak keep, weak drop, or drop. Also marked some for top quality (we really MUST keep), and some that are tricky edge cases to test the extraction. ---
How the docs were selected **Document selection.** The core of the dev set is a *disagreement-and-topicality* sample from a 10,000-WARC CommonCrawl pool: for each held-out eval example that `high_quality` scored worse on than DCLM/Nemotron, we built a keyword fingerprint and selected corpus documents containing ≥3 and ≥80% of that example's keywords, then joined each to a membership table recording every pipeline's keep/drop decision (hq, DCLM, Nemotron-CC, FineWeb-Edu, FineWeb-CC) and stratified the draw by (register × cross-pipeline agreement × hq's own decision) so both kept and dropped documents appear in every register. We then supplemented this with an unbiased uniform sample from a 2013–2026 CommonCrawl timeline, targeted raw-HTML scans that recover code/table pages (via `
`/``/`` and
syntax-highlighter signatures that extraction destroys), diverse general-forum threads, mined
hard-negatives, and the highest-confidence documents DCLM keeps but hq drops.

**Register identification.** Registers were first assigned by domain — each URL reduced to its
registered domain (eTLD+1) and matched against a hand-curated, priority-ordered list of
domain-substring patterns per register — but because that mis-binned platform domains (e.g. a
chemistry article on `geeksforgeeks`, a novel e-text on `gradesaver`), every document was subsequently
re-classified by *content*, with an LLM reading the extracted text and assigning the register it
actually belongs to.

I did do some preliminary experiments to explore if the data mix was the core driver of the problems we are seeing.  I don't think it is, however I didn't do this experiment super carefully (see below):

---



Data Mix and Epoching Tests

hq is the most *permissive* extractor (keeps the most URLs) but the most *diluted* corpus
(85.7% generic "other" vs DCLM's ~72%; knowledge char-share 1.69% vs DCLM 2.77%). Two
mechanisms could explain the gap at fixed compute:

| # | hypothesis | variant | what it changes | holds fixed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C | **density/composition** | `hq_reweight` | mixes full hq (w=0.856) + a knowledge-dense `hq_dense` cache (w=0.144) -> dense char-share **12.3%->25%** (= DCLM) | token budget |
| B | **epochs/repetition** | `hq_epoch` | uniform 34.4% subsample -> **7.33B tokens** (= DCLM's count), so more epochs per token | composition |



Did not work when we unweighted or epoched but we did this in a super naive way...

---



How we defined knowledge-dense

How the `hq_dense` reweight bucket was defined in the Phase-2 dilution ablation
(`experiments/baseline_collection/build_hq_variants.py`).

A doc was counted as **dense** iff its **registered domain** contained one of the substring
patterns below — i.e. `categorize(url) in {reference_wiki, academic, blog, news, qa_help}`.
This is a **domain-only heuristic** (never reads page text); patterns are **priority-ordered**,
first match wins, else `other`. Source of truth: `CATEGORY_PATTERNS` in
`experiments/baseline_collection/provenance_audit_10k.py`.

The five "fact-bearing expository" registers were chosen to mirror what DCLM over-represents
(knowledge-gap decomposition: reference_wiki 2.4×, blog 2.6×, academic 1.7× char-share vs hq).
This subset was ~12% of hq tokens; mixed back at weight 0.144 it lifted the dense char-share
~12% → 25% (matching DCLM) at a fixed token budget.

## reference_wiki (11 patterns)

```
wikipedia, wikia, fandom, wiktionary, wikihow, wikimedia, wikinews, wikibooks, britannica, wikidot, wikispaces
```

## academic (22 patterns)

```
arxiv, biorxiv, ssrn, researchgate, academia.edu, jstor, sciencedirect, springer, ncbi.nlm.nih, plos, pubmed, semanticscholar, citeseerx, iopscience, ieee, acm.org, aps.org, mdpi, tandfonline, wiley, oup.com, sagepub
```

## blog (12 patterns)

```
blogspot, wordpress, tumblr, typepad, medium.com, livejournal, blogs., blog., ghost.io, substack, wixsite, weebly
```

## news (29 patterns)

```
bbc., cnn., nytimes, theguardian, reuters, washingtonpost, forbes, bloomberg, huffpost, huffingtonpost, npr.org, apnews, aljazeera, telegraph, dailymail, foxnews, nbcnews, cbsnews, usatoday, wsj., economist, theatlantic, politico, news, tribune, gazette, herald, chron., latimes
```

## qa_help (6 patterns)

```
answers., ask., support., help., faq, howto
```

## Caveats

- **Plain substring match on the domain** — over- and under-catches. Generic `news` grabs any
  domain containing "news"; `faq` / `howto` are bare substrings that can match mid-domain;
  `blog` is really the *platform* (blogspot/wordpress), whose content is heterogeneous.
- **Domain-only, no text** — "academic" is genuinely journal/preprint domains, but expository
  *quality* within blog/news is unresolved. So the reweight concentrated these **registers by
  domain**, not fact-dense text — a coarse proxy, and part of why the reweight moved nothing.

Might be useful once we switch the the larger pipeline and start training on way more tokens.
---
Finalizing Devset A register-stratified sample of 1,934 CommonCrawl pages (raw HTML + provenance), each judged **keep / weak_keep / weak_drop / drop** for whether it's worth keeping as LM training data. Each doc also carries the keep/drop decisions of the production quality filters (DCLM, Nemotron, FineWeb-Edu/CC, `hq`) so any curation spec can be scored (P/R/F1) against human judgment, overall and per register. **Column key** — *hand-labeled*: judged by a human · *judge*: filled by an LLM judge (sonnet, calibrated to the human labels) where un-hand-labeled · *keep-%*: share labeled keep or weak_keep (i.e. worth training on) · *gold-extraction*: also has a human-verified reference plain-text extraction (the "correct" cleaned content, for scoring extractors) · *top-quality* (★, 134) & *benchmark* (⚑, 242): human flags marking exemplary keeps / good extractor test cases. # Weekly Sync 7/20 - 7/24

---

<details>
<summary>Current Specs I am trying out</summary>

There are now two types of systems I am operating with.  **Multi-Stage** and **Single Stage**.  The Multi-Stage system has a first spec which is just for filtering (reasoning on) and the second stage is extraction from html for pages that are kept.  Single Stage does both and must keep reasoning on for both.  As a result, **multi-stage is approximately 3x faster to run**.

| Spec | Stage | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **high_quality** | Single stage | One-prompt extraction with hard gates (English, ≥300 prose words) + positive criteria; deliberately strict, keeps ~1 in 10 pages. |
| **med_quality** | Single stage | One-prompt extraction with a looser-than-HQ quality bar that still filters nav/boilerplate, fragments, commerce, and incoherent pages. |
| **high_quality_v2** | Multi stage | Basically high_quality but two-stage (filter/quality-gate call, then a separate extraction call); better on fiction and QA/forum content. |
| **llm_pipeline_v1** | Multi stage | Two-stage: a filter/voting gate call, then a separate head + continuation extraction call. |
| **llm_simple_v1** | Single stage | The one-call variant — judging and extraction merged into a single call (plus a continuation call only for long docs). |


---

<details>
<summary>High Quality (my old spec)</summary>

```
[[ ## html ## ]]
{example}

[[ ## extraction_spec ## ]]
Extract the content from this HTML page as clean text. Apply all rules below.

1. **EXTREME quality bar — keep almost nothing.** This filter is designed to retain only the very best educational and informative content; only about 1 in 10 pages should pass. The **default is to output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]**.

   **HARD GATES — check first, in order. If any gate fails, immediately output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and stop.**
   - **Gate A — Language.** Is the body of the page written primarily in English? If the main prose is in any other language (French, Spanish, German, Chinese, Russian, etc.), output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]. Quoted phrases, names, citations, or short snippets in another language are fine; a page whose main prose is non-English is not — even if the topic looks substantive.
   - **Gate B — Prose depth.** Are there roughly 300 or more words of real *prose* — flowing sentences and paragraphs that explain, argue, or teach? Table cells, formula tokens, code-only listings, navigation labels, whois fields, stat lines, and metadata do NOT count toward the word budget. A page that hits 300 "words" only by counting structured-data fields fails this gate.

   A page that clears both gates is kept ONLY if all four of these are also true:

   - **Teaches the reader.** The page explains a concept, mechanism, method, or topic; develops an argument with evidence and examples; reports original analysis; or delivers substantive technical or instructional material. It must convey real knowledge of the world, not just headlines, facts, or summaries.
   - **Carefully written.** Clear, structured, professional or academic-quality prose. Not casual, not fragmentary, not marketing copy, not auto-generated, not template-filled.
   - **Self-contained value.** A reader who lands here learns meaningfully from this page alone — not from clicking through to something else.
   - **Not matched by any FAILS bullet below.**

   **Walk through each FAILS bullet below in order**, checking whether the page matches it. If any matches, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and do not extract.

   Categories that typically qualify (still subject to all criteria above):
   - Long-form journalism with original reporting and analysis — including editorial tech journalism or product reporting that includes quotes, context, history, or analysis (even when the subject is a company's product launch)
   - Educational or explanatory articles (science, math, history, engineering, medicine, philosophy, economics, etc.)
   - Tutorials, how-tos, and documentation with real teaching — instructions plus the reasoning behind them
   - Encyclopedia and reference entries written with substantive prose
   - **Substantive technical forum, mailing-list, or Q&A threads** — e.g., a Stack Overflow question with a thorough accepted answer, a numpy/scipy mailing-list discussion working through a real problem, a developer forum thread that reaches a meaningful technical conclusion. The "casual forum threads" FAILS bullet does NOT apply when the discussion is technical and develops the topic.
   - Research papers, white papers, technical writeups
   - Essays and analyses that develop an argument with evidence — including substantive opinion or commentary on a personal blog or social platform like Tumblr/Medium/Substack
   - Code accompanied by genuine teaching, not just a snippet
   - Technical blogs sharing real domain expertise
   - Institutional or organizational descriptions with substantive prose (academic program pages with curriculum and outcomes, organizational reports, conference or event summaries with real narrative)
   - Religious or scriptural texts presenting substantive narrative or doctrine (e.g., a Bible chapter, Quran sura, philosophical canon — numbered-verse format is fine)

   Categories that FAIL — filter even if the writing is fine:
   - **News briefs, sports recaps, and transaction roundups** — "X happened, said Y" reporting without analysis, depth, or context. Includes local sports recaps ("West Side beat Cumberland 14-4"), team transaction logs ("Signed pitcher X to a minor-league contract"), and short news items even when several are stitched together on one page.
   - **Personal lifestyle or diary blogging** — daily-life updates, travelogues, opinion pieces without intellectual substance. (A personal blog with substantive analysis or argument is fine — judge by content, not platform.)
   - **Light reviews — including aggregator pages of light reviews** — "I tried it, it's good" without genuine analysis or comparison. A page that strings together several short product blurbs is still light reviews, not substantive content.
   - **Reference stubs and structured-data dumps** — one-paragraph wiki entries, definitions, factoid lists, player stat cards, whois/BGP/DNS records, raw lookup results, single-formula pages. If the page is mostly a table, a record, or one isolated fact, it fails — fastText-style classifiers may rate this content highly because it "looks structured," but it is not teaching prose.
   - **Casual forum threads** — chit-chat, brief Q&A without resolution, social exchanges that don't reach a meaningful conclusion. Technical mailing-list or Q&A threads that DO develop the topic are covered by the qualifying bullet above and are NOT this.
   - **Vendor sales copy or purely promotional material** — product descriptions, ad copy, "buy now" pages. (Institutional descriptions of academic programs, mission statements with real content, organizational reports, or editorial journalism about a product launch are NOT this; judge by whether the page sells a product or describes/teaches.)
   - **Mostly un-decoded HTML / escape soup** — pages where the visible text is dominated by raw HTML entities (` `, `<`, `&`, `&#NNN;`), escape sequences, or malformed markup that survived the page render. Even if the underlying content might be code or text, a page presented this way is junk for training.
   - **"No results" / search-empty pages** — "your search returned no results", "no items match", "0 records found" — even when they list related links or alternative searches alongside.
   - **Anything that fails a normal quality filter** — commerce pages, navigation or aggregation surfaces, login walls or other site machinery, fragments and microposts, wrappers around non-textual media, raw data dumps, empty placeholders, incoherent text

   **When in doubt, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT].** Reject borderline pages aggressively; only clear winners pass.

First determine if the page clears the EXTREME quality bar. If it does, follow the following rules to extract the content.

2. **Extract the full page content in reading order**. Keep explanatory text, discussion, and comments that add substantive information. Begin your output directly with the page content.
3. **Remove boilerplate**: navigation, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs, cookie banners, and UI elements. Do not output framework markers or metadata tags.
4. **Preserve all technical content** exactly as written: code, math, formulas, tables, and data. Preserve original line breaks and the structure of code blocks.
5. Decode HTML entities to plain characters (e.g. & → &, ’ → '). Remove raw HTML tags.
6. **Do not add, invent, or embellish content.** Every sentence must come from the source page.
7. For pages with multiple authors or speakers (forums, reviews, comments), preserve who said what — include usernames or speaker labels.
8. If the page contains content spinner templates like {{word1|word2|word3}}, pick the first option. If most of the page is spinners, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT].

Respond with the corresponding output fields, starting with the field `[[ ## text ## ]]`, and then ending with the marker for `[[ ## completed ## ]]`.
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Medium Quality (another old spec)</summary>

```
[[ ## html ## ]]
{example}

[[ ## extraction_spec ## ]]
Extract the content from this HTML page as clean text. Apply all rules below.

1. **Quality bar.** The page must be real written content — coherent prose that conveys information, ideas, narrative, or experience. Acceptable: articles, explanations, analyses, reviews with substantive commentary, tutorials, manuals, reference entries, documentation, and substantive forum or comment discussions. If the page does not pass, output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT].

   **Walk through each bullet below in order**, checking whether the page matches it. If any bullet applies, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and do not extract.

   - **Navigation or aggregation** — exists to point elsewhere (forum indexes, category pages, tag clouds, search results, sitemaps, archive-by-date pages, contributor lists, topic-aggregation pages of one-line summaries). A tag archive showing one truncated post excerpt still fails — the page must contain at least one full post.
   - **Site machinery** — login, signup, paywall, cookie banner, captcha, error page, "page not found", redirect notice, terms of service, privacy policy, subscription/notification form ("send to a friend", email signup), or instructions for using the site itself. Pages whose main content is hidden behind a login wall fail even when the page shows a "you must be logged in" prompt.
   - **Fragments** — Tumblr-style image-reblog streams, social timelines, photo-blog feeds, lists of one-liner microposts, image gallery captions, personal "about me" pages, and repost stubs that consist of a brief excerpt plus a "Read on:", "Go to Source", "View original", or affiliate link to elsewhere. Pages of fragments and metadata rather than coherent passages.
   - **Wrapper around non-textual media** — a video, audio, slideshow, photo, or interactive widget where the page exists to host the media rather than be read. Includes image-only social posts (Blingee/Pinterest-style), single-photo pages with a one-line caption, video-player pages with only a title/byline around the video, and blog posts whose body is a short reaction (a sentence or two) around an embedded video, image, or share.
   - **Commerce or product page** — pages with prices, availability, "Add to Cart", or shipping/stock indicators. Vendor-written descriptions, specs, ingredients, and care instructions are commerce metadata, not content — they do not save the page. Keep only if the page contains an extended editorial passage about the product (a third-party review, comparison, or analysis), not vendor sales copy. Also includes **employer or company profile pages** ("Quick Look", "Company Overview") that are mostly company name, industry, size, and a bullet list of services or job categories.
   - **Raw data dump** — structured data without surrounding narrative. This includes both rows of data (rosters, statistics tables, file indexes, contact directories, database exports) **and single-record entries** (museum specimen cards, IP whois / BGP route lookups, dictionary entries that are only a definition line, badge / user-profile / member pages). An article that uses tables to support its prose is fine.
   - **Too short** — count the substantive sentences on the page after removing boilerplate, navigation, ads, comments, links, dates, and reposted excerpts. **If the remaining substantive prose is fewer than 5 complete sentences, the page fails.** Apply this strictly: a 1-paragraph news brief, a 2-sentence "X just opened in Y" announcement, a single-event calendar entry, "this section has moved" notice, "no results found" / "no products matching" / "click here to proceed" placeholder — all fail, regardless of how grammatical or informative-looking the few sentences are.
   - **Incoherent** — gibberish, garbled encoding, machine-translated nonsense, or spinner templates throughout.

First determine if the page clears the quality bar. If it does, follow the following rules to extract the content.

2. **Extract the full page content in reading order**. Keep explanatory text, discussion, and comments that add substantive information. Begin your output directly with the page content.
3. **Remove boilerplate**: navigation, footers, sidebars, ads, share buttons, related links, breadcrumbs, cookie banners, and UI elements. Do not output framework markers or metadata tags.
4. **Preserve all technical content** exactly as written: code, math, formulas, tables, and data. Preserve original line breaks and the structure of code blocks.
5. Decode HTML entities to plain characters (e.g. & → &, ’ → '). Remove raw HTML tags.
6. **Do not add, invent, or embellish content.** Every sentence must come from the source page.
7. For pages with multiple authors or speakers (forums, reviews, comments), preserve who said what — include usernames or speaker labels.
8. If the page contains content spinner templates like {{word1|word2|word3}}, pick the first option. If most of the page is spinners, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT].

Respond with the corresponding output fields, starting with the field `[[ ## text ## ]]`, and then ending with the marker for `[[ ## completed ## ]]`.
```

</details>

---

<details>
<summary>LLM Pipeline V1</summary>

**Filter**
```
You are given the plain text of a web page, with its HTML removed. Decide whether the page belongs in a high-quality text corpus. This is a judgement, not an extraction: do not reproduce the page.

FIRST, quote a few words from the page's main text and name the human language they are written in. Source code counts as English. If the language is not English, output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and stop.

THE READER TEST: imagine someone who came to this page on purpose. Would they READ it — start at the top of its text and follow it to the end — or would they LOOK IT OVER and click somewhere else?

Pages people read: articles, stories, explanations, tutorials, arguments, answers with their questions, discussions worth following, reference entries that explain, code — a source file is read by a programmer the way an article is read by anyone else — and study material: flashcards, vocabulary sets and revision notes are studied line by line, which is reading.

Pages people look over: photo and video pages, galleries, profile cards, product pages, schedules and calendars, search results, link lists, archives of teasers — teasers are posts cut short with a "read more" link; a page carrying several COMPLETE posts in full, one after another, is not an archive of teasers, it is writing, and it is read, login screens, records from a database, and pages made of ENTRIES — dictionary definitions, cast and credit lists, arrest blotters, specimen records: entries are looked up, not read, however many there are. Add to these the pages that serve a moment instead of a reader: event announcements with their date-time-place details, notices that a page has moved, calls for donations or signups, and posts whose text exists to present something else — a photo set, a video, a track, an episode, a craft project: text that presents media is looked over, and the writer's enthusiasm does not make it an article.

A page someone would read belongs in the corpus. A page someone would only look over does not — no matter how well written its labels are. If the page holds both, judge by what a visitor came for: a real article above its comment form is read; a photo above its caption is looked at.

Do not drop writing for being short or plain: a complete short answer is read. Fiction is read, including adult-themed fiction; only text existing to be sexually explicit fails.

One more tell: strip away the moment. If the page exists to serve a live instant — an event coming up, a sale running, a notice posted, a record logged today — ask whether it would still inform a stranger who found it after that moment passed. A page whose whole job ends with its moment is looked over, not read.

If the page would be read, output exactly: KEEP
Otherwise output exactly: [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]
```

**Extraction**
```
Extract this web page's content as clean plain text. You are given a MIDDLE OR END SECTION of a long page whose beginning was already processed and judged worth keeping. This section can begin or end mid-sentence; that is expected. Extract what is in front of you, in the order it appears.

Extract only what this page is about: its article, its story, its thread, its question and the answers to it. Around that, pages show pointers to other pages — "related" or "popular" link lists, teasers and headlines of other articles, archives of past posts, lists of other questions. Those are pointers, not content: leave them out.

KEEP the content a reader came to this page for: articles, news stories, blog posts, essays, fiction and stories, explanations, tutorials, reference material, the question and its answers, the thread's posts and comments, code with its explanation, mathematics (keep LaTeX), data tables and statistics, product reviews, and scientific, medical, legal, historical, or educational writing.

REMOVE page furniture: navigation menus, headers, footers, sidebars, search boxes, forms, ads, cookie banners, newsletter prompts, share buttons, related-link lists, breadcrumbs, and repeated boilerplate.

Begin your output directly with the content. If this section is entirely page furniture with no content in it, output nothing at all.
```

</details>

---

<details>
<summary>LLM Simple V1</summary>

```
You are given the HTML source of a web page (scripts and styles stripped). Decide whether the page belongs in a high-quality text corpus; if it does, output its content as clean plain text. You may be given the whole page or one section of a long page — a section can begin or end mid-sentence; that is expected.

FIRST, quote a few words from the main text and name their language; if not English (code counts as English), output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and stop. THEN apply the reader test: would a visitor READ this page start to end, or LOOK IT OVER and click away? Galleries, listings, product pages, search results, archives of teasers, profiles, login screens and event notices are looked over — output exactly [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and stop. Articles, stories, tutorials, discussions, Q&A and code are read.

If the page would be read, output its content as clean plain text:
- Keep the content a reader came for: articles, stories, explanations, tutorials, reference material, the question and its answers, the thread's posts and comments with their usernames and dates, code with its explanation, mathematics (keep LaTeX), data tables and statistics.
- Leave out the furniture and the pointers: navigation menus, headers, footers, sidebars, search boxes, forms, ads, cookie banners, newsletter prompts, share buttons, "related" and "popular" link lists, teasers for other pages, breadcrumbs, and repeated boilerplate.
- Reproduce the kept text faithfully: the same words in the same order, no summarizing, no rewriting, no added formatting syntax (no markdown headings, no ** bold, no [link](url) notation).
- Begin your output directly with the page content. If this section is entirely furniture, output nothing at all.
```

</details>

---

<details>
<summary>High Quality V2</summary>

**Filter**:
```
You are given the text of a web page. Decide whether it clears the EXTREME quality bar below. This is a judgement only — do not extract or reproduce the page.

The text is a mechanical rendering of the page: a forum thread, Q&A page, or comment section appears as a flat sequence of posts — usernames and timestamps followed by each post's text, with paragraph structure flattened. Judge the DISCUSSION those posts form, not the flatness of the rendering: Gate B's prose requirement is met by the posts' combined substantive text, and a substantive multi-post discussion is not "casual" merely because its rendering looks like short lines. Navigation labels and UI text in the rendering are page furniture — ignore them when judging. Likewise, mathematical notation renders here as flattened runs of symbols — those runs ARE mathematical exposition for Gate B's exception, not junk; and a research paper's abstract often sits below rendered site chrome — find the abstract and judge it, not the chrome around it.

1. **EXTREME quality bar — keep almost nothing.** This filter is designed to retain only the very best educational and informative content; only about 1 in 10 pages should pass. The **default is to output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]**.

   **HARD GATES — check first, in order. If any gate fails, immediately output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and stop.**
   - **Gate A — Language.** Is the body of the page written primarily in English? If the main prose is in any other language (French, Spanish, German, Chinese, Russian, etc.), output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT]. Quoted phrases, names, citations, or short snippets in another language are fine; a page whose main prose is non-English is not — even if the topic looks substantive.
   - **Gate B — Prose depth.** Are there roughly 300 or more words of real *prose* — flowing sentences and paragraphs that explain, argue, or teach? Table cells, formula tokens, code-only listings, navigation labels, whois fields, stat lines, and metadata do NOT count toward the word budget. A page that hits 300 "words" only by counting structured-data fields fails this gate. **Exception — substance in non-prose forms.** Three content types carry their teaching outside flowing prose and pass this gate with less than 300 prose words, provided the content is complete and substantive: (a) mathematical exposition whose formulas, derivations, and worked steps ARE the content; (b) a research-paper abstract page presenting a complete abstract of substantial density; (c) practice problems or exam material accompanied by worked solutions or answer explanations. A bare formula, a title-only abstract stub, or an answer key without explanations still fails.

   A page that clears both gates is kept ONLY if all four of these are also true:

   - **Teaches the reader — or is literature.** The page explains a concept, mechanism, method, or topic; develops an argument with evidence and examples; reports original analysis; delivers substantive technical or instructional material; **or is fiction/literary narrative of real craft (see the fiction category below — literature earns its place by its writing, not by teaching)**. It must convey real knowledge of the world or real literary value, not just headlines, facts, or summaries.
   - **Carefully written.** Clear, structured, professional or academic-quality prose. Not casual, not fragmentary, not marketing copy, not auto-generated, not template-filled.
   - **Self-contained value.** A reader who lands here learns meaningfully from this page alone — not from clicking through to something else.
   - **Not matched by any FAILS bullet below.**

   **Walk through each FAILS bullet below in order**, checking whether the page matches it. If any matches, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] and do not extract.

   Categories that typically qualify (still subject to all criteria above):
   - Long-form journalism with original reporting and analysis — including editorial tech journalism or product reporting that includes quotes, context, history, or analysis (even when the subject is a company's product launch)
   - Educational or explanatory articles (science, math, history, engineering, medicine, philosophy, economics, etc.)
   - Tutorials, how-tos, and documentation with real teaching — instructions plus the reasoning behind them
   - Encyclopedia and reference entries written with substantive prose
   - **Substantive discussion threads — technical or not** — e.g., a Stack Overflow question with a thorough accepted answer, a mailing-list discussion working through a real problem, a history or law or hobbyist forum thread where participants bring real knowledge and the discussion develops its topic to a meaningful conclusion. Conversational tone does not disqualify a thread; judge what the discussion BUILDS, not how informally it speaks. The "casual forum threads" FAILS bullet does NOT apply when the discussion develops its topic.
   - Research papers, white papers, technical writeups
   - Essays and analyses that develop an argument with evidence — including substantive opinion or commentary on a personal blog or social platform like Tumblr/Medium/Substack
   - Code accompanied by genuine teaching, not just a snippet
   - Technical blogs sharing real domain expertise
   - Institutional or organizational descriptions with substantive prose (academic program pages with curriculum and outcomes, organizational reports, conference or event summaries with real narrative)
   - Religious or scriptural texts presenting substantive narrative or doctrine (e.g., a Bible chapter, Quran sura, philosophical canon — numbered-verse format is fine)
   - **Fiction and literary narrative of real craft** — complete stories, novel chapters, serialized fiction installments, and literary prose whose writing is skilled and whose narrative is substantial. Judge it as literature, not as instruction: fiction does not need to teach a concept; it needs to be genuinely well-written and substantial. Adult themes do not disqualify fiction, but text that exists to be sexually explicit is not literature and fails. Fragments, writing-exercise scraps, and story stubs still fail.

   Categories that FAIL — filter even if the writing is fine:
   - **News briefs, sports recaps, and transaction roundups** — "X happened, said Y" reporting without analysis, depth, or context. Includes local sports recaps ("West Side beat Cumberland 14-4"), team transaction logs ("Signed pitcher X to a minor-league contract"), and short news items even when several are stitched together on one page. A news article that goes beyond the event — developing background, quotes woven into narrative, or consequences analyzed — is journalism, not a brief; brevity alone does not make a brief, and analysis does not stop being analysis because its subject is timely.
   - **Personal lifestyle or diary blogging** — daily-life updates, travelogues, opinion pieces without intellectual substance. (A personal blog with substantive analysis or argument is fine — judge by content, not platform.)
   - **Light reviews — including aggregator pages of light reviews** — "I tried it, it's good" without genuine analysis or comparison. A page that strings together several short product blurbs is still light reviews, not substantive content.
   - **Reference stubs and structured-data dumps** — one-paragraph wiki entries, definitions, factoid lists, player stat cards, whois/BGP/DNS records, raw lookup results, single-formula pages. If the page is mostly a table, a record, or one isolated fact, it fails — fastText-style classifiers may rate this content highly because it "looks structured," but it is not teaching prose.
   - **Casual forum threads** — chit-chat, brief Q&A without resolution, social exchanges that don't reach a meaningful conclusion. This bullet is about SUBSTANCE, not tone: an informal thread that genuinely develops its topic is covered by the qualifying bullet above and is NOT this; a polite thread that builds nothing is.
   - **Vendor sales copy or purely promotional material** — product descriptions, ad copy, "buy now" pages. (Institutional descriptions of academic programs, mission statements with real content, organizational reports, or editorial journalism about a product launch are NOT this; judge by whether the page sells a product or describes/teaches.)
   - **Mostly un-decoded HTML / escape soup** — pages where the visible text is dominated by raw HTML entities (` `, `<`, `&`, `&#NNN;`), escape sequences, or malformed markup that survived the page render. Even if the underlying content might be code or text, a page presented this way is junk for training.
   - **"No results" / search-empty pages** — "your search returned no results", "no items match", "0 records found" — even when they list related links or alternative searches alongside.
   - **Anything that fails a normal quality filter** — commerce pages, navigation or aggregation surfaces, login walls or other site machinery, fragments and microposts, wrappers around non-textual media, raw data dumps, empty placeholders, incoherent text

   **When in doubt, output [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT].** Reject borderline pages aggressively; only clear winners pass.

Output exactly one of:
- KEEP — the page clears every gate and criterion above
- [NO_USEFUL_CONTENT] — anything else.
```

**Extract:**
```

https://claude.ai/code/artifact/344c5a6c-2da1-44ef-87c7-2b4e978f154f 

**Benchmark numbers are promising but don't paint this as a slam dunk:**



Custom Metrics

Three numbers for "did the extraction keep the page's content, and nothing else."
Everything is computed on **normalized** text, so markdown, emphasis, quotes,
dashes, whitespace and rendered-vs-LaTeX math (`κ` = `\kappa`) never count as a
difference.

Let $G$ be the gold text and $P$ the prediction.

- $S(x)$ = the **set of 5-grams** of $\text{normalize}(x)$
- $U(G)$ = the **sentences of $G$** with at least 8 words

## KEPT — recall

Fraction of gold's sentences that survive. A sentence counts as kept if at least
half of its 5-grams appear anywhere in the prediction:

$$\text{KEPT} = \frac{1}{|U(G)|}\sum_{u \in U(G)} \mathbb{1}\!\left[\frac{|S(u) \cap S(P)|}{|S(u)|} \ge 0.5\right]$$

Sentences shorter than 5 words can't form a 5-gram, so they're matched by direct
substring containment instead.

## CLEAN — precision

Fraction of what we emitted that actually exists in gold:

$$\text{CLEAN} = \frac{|S(P) \cap S(G)|}{|S(P)|}$$

## FIDELITY — the headline

F-score of the two, with **recall weighted twice as heavily** as precision
($\beta^2 = 2$), because dropping content is worse than keeping extra:

$$\text{FIDELITY} = \frac{(1+\beta^2)\cdot \text{CLEAN} \cdot \text{KEPT}}{\beta^2 \cdot \text{CLEAN} + \text{KEPT}} = \frac{3\cdot \text{CLEAN}\cdot \text{KEPT}}{2\cdot \text{CLEAN} + \text{KEPT}}$$

The same construction gives **CODE**, **MATH**, **TABLE** and **WHO** — identical
to KEPT, but with $U(G)$ replaced by gold's code lines, math expressions, table
cells, or speaker names.




Overall I think our new spec is better but it wasn't as easy to hill climb this as I had hoped.

# Weekly Sync 8/31-9/4 ---
"Hero" Data Curation Run Progress We currently have about 10T tokens of pre-dedupe data processed! This will be significantly lower after dedupe, but dedupe alone now takes many hours (days?) to run, so I don't have timely feedback about how much data we have post-dedupe. **Updated this morning:**
> [!TIP] > The run is about 15% of the way through and will finish in the next 2 weeks if I don't steal my compute for other experiments. ---
More principled FLOP estimation ## Inference FLOPs of the fast curation cascade **Estimate: 1.3e10 to 1.7e10 FLOPs per extracted document, 5.1e14 to 6.7e14 per WARC, and 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 for the 8M-WARC run (7,925,398 WARCs).** The low end charges each document its real token count; the high end charges the padded length the chip actually runs. ettin68 accounts for 98% of the total. | | Actual lengths | Padded lengths | |---|---|---| | Per extracted doc | 1.3e10 | 1.7e10 | | Per kept doc | 6.9e10 | 9.0e10 | | Per WARC | 5.1e14 | 6.7e14 | | Per kept token (ModernBERT tokens) | 5.1e7 | 6.7e7 | | 8M run total | 4.0e21 | 5.3e21 | The rest of this note explains how the numbers are produced. The deployed pipeline (`lpv11_fastpipe_v2_1_fused`) scores every extracted document with three classifiers in sequence: fastText, a pooled super-token transformer, and ettin68. Each stage only sees the documents the previous stage passed on, so the cost per document is an expectation over the stages a document reaches. ### Stages and reach rates | Stage | Model | Context | Condition to run | Share of extracted docs | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | fastText w640 | full doc | always | 100% | | 2 | pooled transformer (90M-doc ckpt) | 8192 | fastText prob ≥ 0.0048 | 58.2% | | 3 | ettin68 | 2048 | pooled prob in [0.079, 0.8883) | 20.1% | Of the documents the pooled model scores, 18.3% are accepted outright, 47.2% are dropped, and 34.6% go to ettin68. Overall, 19.2% of extracted documents are kept. Rates are measured from production catalogs (52 shards, 12,824 WARCs). Per WARC: 39,464 records, 38,560 extracted docs, 22,423 fastText survivors, 7,749 band docs, 7,413 kept docs. ## Expected cost per document ``` E[FLOPs per extracted doc] = c_ft + p_ft * E[ c_pool(min(L, 8192)) | passed fastText ] + p_ft * p_band * E[ c_ettin(min(L, 2048)) | in band ] p_ft = 0.5815 p_band = 0.3456 ``` Each stage's cost is averaged over the token-length distribution of the documents that actually reach it. Those distributions come from the 100k comparison sample, which stores every stage's score per document: we tokenize its deployment text with the ModernBERT tokenizer and apply the production thresholds. The sample's reach rates match production within two points. **How padding works.** Within a WARC, the scorer sorts a stage's documents by length, takes batches of 32, and pads each batch to the smallest bucket in (128, 256, ..., context) that fits the longest document in that batch. The last batch is filled to 32 rows with empty rows. Because batches are length-sorted, all 32 documents in a batch are close in length, so the padded cost is well approximated by charging each document its own bucket; simulating the real per-batch procedure on the sample gives the same mean within 1%. Padding raises the mean charged length by 1.37x for the pooled stage and 1.30x for ettin68, which is the gap between the two columns below and in the headline table. | Stage | Reach rate | Mean tokens, actual (capped at context) | Mean tokens, padded | Cost per doc, actual | Cost per doc, padded | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | fastText | 100% | 1,318 (no cap) | n/a | 2.0e5 | 2.0e5 | | pooled | 58.2% | 1,010 | 1,380 | 4.1e8 | 5.7e8 | | ettin68 | 20.1% | 608 | 792 | 6.5e10 | 8.5e10 | ## 8M run document counts (7,925,398 WARCs) | | Count | |---|---| | Docs scored by fastText | 3.1e11 | | Docs scored by pooled | 1.8e11 | | Docs scored by ettin68 | 6.1e10 | | Kept docs | 5.9e10 | For reference, 4.0e21 to 5.3e21 FLOPs is the 6ND training cost of a 1B model on 700B to 900B tokens. ## Caveats - FLOPs and chip time diverge. Measured chip time from the catalogs implies MFU of 0.1 to 0.4% for the pooled stage and 1.4 to 5.7% for ettin68. All-in, the run is 26.2 v6e-8 slice-seconds per WARC (about 58k slice-hours for 8M WARCs), which is 0.35% MFU against the FLOP total. - fastText FLOPs count arithmetic only. Its measured cost is 0.55 CPU-ms per document, mostly hashing and table lookups. - Token counts use the ModernBERT tokenizer, not the training tokenizer. - Reach rates are from the current ladder's crawl mix.
Conventions - Forward pass only; a multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs. - Embedding lookups, layer norms, softmax, activations, and the pooling reduction count as zero. - Length `L` includes the two special tokens and is capped at the stage context. The padded variant rounds `L` up to the next bucket in (128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192). - Empty tail rows in a WARC's last batch are included in the per-batch simulation and add under 1%.
fastText formula dim 100, word bigrams, no character n-grams (read from the model header). Features are words plus bigrams, about twice the word count; words are taken as 0.75 of ModernBERT tokens. One add per dimension per feature, then a 100 x 2 output layer. ``` F = 2 * 0.75 * T c_ft = 100 * F + 2 * 100 * 2 ≈ 150 T + 400 ``` At T = 1,318 this is 2.0e5.
Pooled transformer formula Levanter's `PooledTransformerConfig.flops_per_token`, called directly. `L` padded tokens, `S = L / 64` super-tokens, hidden `D = 512`, pooled input width 768 (mean, max, min of 256-dim embeddings), feed-forward 2048, 4 layers, 2 labels. ``` proj = 2 * 768 * D * S layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 * S # q, k, v, o projections + 2 * 2 * S^2 * D # QK^T and AV + 2 * 2 * D * 2048 * S # MLP head = 2 * D * 2 c_pool(L) = proj + 4 * layer + head ``` About 4.1e5 FLOPs per input token, nearly flat in `L`.
ettin68 formula Hand-derived (Levanter's generic helper adds a vocabulary-head term a classifier does not have). Hidden `D = 512`, GeGLU feed-forward 768, 19 layers, 8 heads, global attention on every third layer starting at layer 0 (7 layers), sliding window 128 on the other 12. ``` linear_per_token_per_layer = 2 * 4 * D^2 # q, k, v, o + 2 * D * 2 * 768 # GeGLU up and gate + 2 * 768 * D # down attn_per_token_per_layer = 4 * span * D # span = L (global), min(L, 128) (local) c_ettin(L) = L * sum over 19 layers of (linear + attn) ``` Linear term 8.5e7 per token (two times the 42M non-embedding parameters); attention 3.2e7 at L = 2048; total 1.17e8 per token.
Data sources - Reach rates and per-WARC counts: fused catalogs, 52 random shards of the 404 to 8079 ladder. - Per-stage length distributions: 100k comparison sample (`extractor_compare/high_quality_200warc`), deployment text tokenized with `answerdotai/ModernBERT-base`, production thresholds applied to stored scores. - Model shapes: checkpoint `config.json` for pooled 90M and ettin68; fastText hyperparameters from the model binary header. - Chip time: catalog columns `pooled_s` and `score_s` times device count, per device type.
> [!TIP] > The distilled pipeline is projected to take about 5e21 flops to run on the full 8M WARC files. > The previous 8B model running on all of the internet was projected to take between 3e25 and 1.8e26 flops depending on if I used the pipeline version or the single call spec. > The fact that it is taking a month is likely somewhat due to poor MFU ---
Updated Main Results from Mixing
> [!TIP] > Finally showing signs of how the "more data" really helps at scale (100B+ tokens) ---
Beta Paper Outline Old Paper: https://www.overleaf.com/read/krtygrzdmrzc#9088c4 New Paper (extremely preliminary for now, will auto-update here): https://www.overleaf.com/read/tzzfngmmyqsp#daf616 **Introduction:** Something about how we should spend way more compute on data curation but it doesn't need to be more complicated. **Background**: Current data curation pipelines including data mixing **Method**: Spec-Driven Curation, as well as the distillation into FastText, Pooled Transformer, and Ettin68 (modernBERT) **Swapping the spec enables control of the data distribution**: We show different specs lead to expected changes in data downstream
Plots
We then argue that because of the mixing and the growing demand for tokens we opt to use the coverage spec. **Spec-Driven Curation Yields Bigger and Better Data**: We show that by using our high coverage spec distilled pipeline we get more data and can mix it to be better at many domains.
Plots **Bigger**: Everything else bends upwards, but we can train on 100B+ tokens from just 10k WARCs. If we 800x (which is a bad way to do this bc no accounting for dedup), then we should be able to train on 80T tokens without issue. **Better Coverage**: We can mix for several downstream target capabilities.
**Ablations**: When we remove parts of the system how much does it impact performance. All ablations will be done on the olmo base easy eval set.
Plots **THESE ARE JUST STAND IN PLOTS, I HAVE TO RUN THESE EXPERIMENTS:** **Original Resiliparse vs Our "AutoResearch" Resiliparse**: **Spec for Quality ("High Quality") vs Spec for Coverage ("High Coverage")**: **Distilled Pipeline into Classifiers vs Original**: **Mixing vs No Mixing**:
**Discussion**: Scaling this up to the full internet **Conclusion**: Invest more flops into the pretraining data curation.
> [!TIP] > I tore apart the old paper but tried to keep the focus around the spec-driven idea. Interested to discuss if this is the right framing :) ---

issues.body:
Profile and evaluate the context-parallel (CP) improvements identified during #9119 review. Keep #9119’s initial hero CP integration bounded; address any demonstrated correctness failure or severe bottleneck before merging it. The items below are follow-up candidates, not established merge blockers.

- **Sliding-window attention:** measure the full K/V gather cost and evaluate gathering only the required left halo. Update global query/key coordinates, packed-document masks, and backward accumulation together. [Review](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9119#discussion_r4075733130).
- **Causal load balance and empty backward tiles:** measure per-shard work with representative packed data and long documents. Evaluate balanced sequence placement separately from safely skipping fully masked backward work. Preserve zero dK/dV writes where required; a bare early return is insufficient. [Review](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9119#discussion_r4075733135).
- **Short-convolution halo copies:** inspect generated code and profiles for concatenate/pad traffic. Evaluate a separate halo input only if the copies materially affect throughput; preserve forward and backward parity across document/shard boundaries. [Review](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9119#discussion_r4075733141).
- **Multiple batch rows per device:** measure token-layout redistribution in dense and routed MLPs, then evaluate retaining batch/local-sequence layout through routing. The single-rack hero configuration has global batch 16 sharded over EP=16, with CP=4 splitting sequence positions, leaving one batch row per device; include a larger local batch in this study. [Review](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9119#discussion_r4075733150).
- **K/V gradient reduction precision:** quantify error from casting each shard's FP32 partials to the input dtype before reduction. Compare with an FP32-reduction variant and assess memory, throughput, and numerical behavior. The documented rounding difference alone does not establish a correctness failure or convergence equivalence. [Review](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9119#discussion_r4075733114).

Done when each item has a linked measurement and disposition (implement in a separate PR or retain the existing design). Any implementation must pass output/gradient parity checks under the existing [testing tolerance policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/AGENTS.md), cover packed boundaries and padding at CP>1, and include CP=1 and CP>1 performance measurements. Target new attention implementation work at the native SM100 adapters in #9228; existing-kernel profiles can still establish baselines.

Part of #8754.
